entities.name: Eochaid mac Echdach
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eochaid mac Echdach, who reigned as king of Dál Riata from 726 until his death in 733 CE, was a pivotal figure during a period of intense dynastic instability and external pressure on the Gaelic kingdom in early medieval Scotland. His reign, though brief, encapsulates the fierce succession struggles that plagued Dál Riata in the early 8th century, ultimately contributing to its subjugation by the rising Pictish power. As a son of Eochaid mac Domangairt, he represented a branch of the Cenél nGabráin, one of the dominant kindreds vying for control.

Eochaid's ascent to the throne was not peaceful, emerging from a destructive civil war following the abdication of Selbach mac Ferchair in 723 CE. His primary rival was Dúngal mac Selbaig, Selbach's son, who had been expelled from Kintyre and subsequently from Dál Riata itself. The "Annals of Ulster" record Dúngal's expulsion of Eochaid from the island of Torach in 727, indicating a continued struggle for supremacy. However, Eochaid eventually secured the kingship, possibly with external support, only to face the formidable Pictish king Óengus I, who systematically dismantled Dál Riata's independence, culminating in the major Pictish victory at the battle of Monith Carno in 728 CE against Dúngal and his allies.

The consequence of Eochaid's reign, and indeed the entire Dál Riata succession crisis, was the severe weakening of the Gaelic kingdom, making it vulnerable to Pictish expansion. While Eochaid maintained a semblance of kingship until 733 CE, his final years were marked by increasing Pictish dominance. The subsequent Pictish campaigns under Óengus I in 736 and 741 CE effectively ended Dál Riata's independent political existence, integrating its territories into the nascent Pictish super-kingdom, a precursor to the eventual Kingdom of Alba.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eochaid mac Echdach's brief reign as King of Dál Riata from 726-733 CE marks a critical phase in the kingdom's decline, directly preceding its subjugation by the Picts and thus significantly influencing the geopolitical formation of early medieval Scotland.
